sources.name: OpenSSF Source Code Management Platform Configuration Best Practices

rules.title: Enterprise authenticates through an identity provider
rules.rationale: With Enterprise Managed Users, the identity provider controls who can sign in, MFA and Conditional Access. GitHub's own two-factor settings do not apply to managed users, so the IdP configuration is the main authentication control.
rules.remediation: Configure OIDC (Entra ID, with Conditional Access Policy support) or SAML for the enterprise, and enforce MFA and device or location conditions in the IdP.
rules.manual_check: Screenshot Enterprise settings > Authentication security, and verify MFA and Conditional Access policies for the GitHub application in the IdP.

rules.title: Access is restricted by IP allow list or Conditional Access
rules.rationale: Without network restrictions, a stolen session or token can be used from anywhere. An IP allow list, or IdP Conditional Access with OIDC, limits where the enterprise can be reached from.
rules.remediation: Enable the enterprise IP allow list, including for installed GitHub Apps, or use OIDC with Conditional Access Policies to restrict access to managed devices and networks.
rules.manual_check: Screenshot Enterprise settings > Authentication security > IP allow list, or document the Conditional Access policy in the IdP.

references.title: Restricting network traffic with an IP allow list

rules.title: Number of enterprise owners is limited
rules.rationale: Enterprise owners control every policy and organization. Each owner account is a high-value target, while a single owner is a single point of failure.
rules.remediation: Keep two to five enterprise owners. Use billing manager and organization roles for everyone else, and review the owner list regularly.

rules.title: Number of organization owners is limited
rules.rationale: Organization owners can change every setting, read every repository and remove protections. Too many owners widen the attack surface; a single owner is a single point of failure.
rules.remediation: Keep two to five owners per organization. Grant narrower access through teams, repository roles, security managers or custom organization roles.

rules.title: Repository admin access is granted through teams
rules.rationale: Admin access given directly to individual users is hard to review and is often left behind when people change roles. Admins can disable branch protection and security features.
rules.remediation: Grant admin access through a team synchronized from the IdP, and remove direct admin collaborators.

rules.title: Outside collaborators are reviewed
rules.rationale: Outside collaborators (repository collaborators in an EMU enterprise) have access to repositories without organization membership, and are easily forgotten in access reviews.
rules.remediation: Review each outside collaborator, remove those no longer needed, and restrict who can invite collaborators.

references.title: Abilities and restrictions of managed user accounts

rules.title: Base repository permission is read or none
rules.rationale: The base permission applies to every member in every repository. Write or admin as the base permission lets any member push to, or reconfigure, every repository.
rules.remediation: Set the base permission to 'No permission' or 'Read' at enterprise level, and grant write access through teams.
rules.manual_check: Screenshot Organization settings > Member privileges > Base permissions.

references.title: Setting base permissions for an organization
Enforcing repository management policies in your enterprise

rules.title: Members cannot change repository visibility
rules.rationale: If members can change visibility, a private repository can be made internal and readable by the whole enterprise by any repository admin, without review.
rules.remediation: Set the enterprise policy for repository visibility changes to organization owners only.
rules.manual_check: If no enterprise policy is set, screenshot Organization settings > Member privileges > Repository visibility change in each organization.

references.title: Enforcing repository management policies in your enterprise

rules.title: Members cannot delete or transfer repositories
rules.rationale: Repository deletion and transfer destroy or move code and history. Only organization owners should be able to do this.
rules.remediation: Set the enterprise policy for repository deletion and transfer to organization owners only.
rules.manual_check: If no enterprise policy is set, screenshot Organization settings > Member privileges > Repository deletion and transfer in each organization.

references.title: Enforcing repository management policies in your enterprise

rules.title: Forking of private and internal repositories is restricted
rules.rationale: Forks keep a copy of the code outside the original repository's access control and protections, and survive when access to the original is removed.
rules.remediation: Disable forking of private and internal repositories at enterprise level, or limit forks to the same organization.

references.title: Managing the forking policy for your organization

rules.title: Members cannot invite outside collaborators
rules.rationale: When any repository admin can add collaborators, access can be granted outside the normal approval and IdP processes.
rules.remediation: Restrict inviting repository collaborators to organization owners at enterprise level.
rules.manual_check: If no enterprise policy is set, screenshot Organization settings > Member privileges > Repository collaborators in each organization.

references.title: Enforcing repository management policies in your enterprise

rules.title: Default branch requires a reviewed pull request
rules.rationale: Without a required review, one compromised account or one mistake can put code directly into the branch that is built and deployed.
rules.remediation: Use an organization ruleset that targets the default branch of all repositories and requires a pull request with at least one approval.

rules.title: Force pushes to the default branch are blocked
rules.rationale: A force push rewrites history. It can remove reviewed commits or hide malicious changes.
rules.remediation: Add the 'Block force pushes' rule to the default-branch ruleset.

rules.title: Default branch cannot be deleted
rules.rationale: Deleting the default branch removes the protected history and breaks builds and deployments.
rules.remediation: Add the 'Restrict deletions' rule to the default-branch ruleset.

rules.title: New commits invalidate earlier approvals
rules.rationale: If approvals survive new pushes, an author can get approval for a harmless change and then push different code before merging.
rules.remediation: Enable 'Dismiss stale pull request approvals when new commits are pushed' or 'Require approval of the most recent reviewable push'.

rules.title: Code owner review is required
rules.rationale: Code owner review ensures that changes to sensitive paths, such as workflows and infrastructure code, are approved by the people responsible for them.
rules.remediation: Add a CODEOWNERS file that covers at least .github/ and infrastructure code, and require code owner review in the default-branch ruleset.

rules.title: Status checks are required before merging
rules.rationale: Required status checks make tests and security scans gate the merge, instead of only reporting after the fact.
rules.remediation: Require the build, test and code scanning checks in the default-branch ruleset.

rules.title: Rule bypass is limited
rules.rationale: Actors who can always bypass rulesets, and administrators exempt from classic branch protection, can push unreviewed code. Bypass should be rare, limited to a few roles, and preferably only through a pull request.
rules.remediation: Limit bypass actors to a small team or role, set bypass mode to 'For pull requests only' where possible, and enable 'Do not allow bypassing the above settings' for classic branch protection.

rules.title: Rule bypasses in the last 30 days are explained
rules.rationale: Each bypass is a push that skipped review or other required rules. Frequent bypasses show that the rules do not fit the workflow, or that they are being circumvented.
rules.remediation: Review each bypass with the actor. Adjust rules or bypass lists so that bypass stays exceptional.
rules.manual_check: Organization settings > Rules > Insights, filtered on bypassed.

rules.title: CODEOWNERS files are valid
rules.rationale: Invalid lines in CODEOWNERS are ignored, so the intended owners are silently not requested for review.
rules.remediation: Fix the reported lines: unknown users or teams, teams without access to the repository, and syntax errors.

rules.title: Only approved actions can run
rules.rationale: Every action runs with the workflow's token and secrets. Allowing all actions lets any repository pull in arbitrary third-party code.
rules.remediation: Allow only actions created by GitHub, verified creators and an approved list, set at enterprise level.

references.title: Enforcing policies for GitHub Actions in your enterprise
Disabling or limiting GitHub Actions for your organization

rules.title: Actions must be pinned to a full commit SHA
rules.rationale: Tags and branches can be moved by the action's owner or an attacker who compromises it, so a tag reference can start running different code without any change in the workflow.
rules.remediation: Enable the policy that requires actions to be pinned to a full-length commit SHA, and use Dependabot to keep the pins up to date.
rules.manual_check: Screenshot Enterprise settings > Policies > Actions, or each organization's Actions settings.

references.title: Actions policy supports blocking and SHA pinning

rules.title: GITHUB_TOKEN is read-only by default
rules.rationale: With write as the default, every workflow, and every action it uses, can push code, create releases and change issues unless it explicitly asks for less.
rules.remediation: Set the default workflow permissions to read at enterprise or organization level, and grant write per job with a permissions block.
rules.manual_check: Screenshot Enterprise settings > Policies > Actions > Workflow permissions.

references.title: Use GITHUB_TOKEN for authentication in workflows

rules.title: GitHub Actions cannot approve pull requests
rules.rationale: If workflows can approve pull requests, a workflow, or anyone who can change one, can satisfy required reviews without a human.
rules.remediation: Disable 'Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull requests'.
rules.manual_check: Screenshot Enterprise settings > Policies > Actions > Workflow permissions.

references.title: Disabling or limiting GitHub Actions for your organization

rules.title: Workflows from fork pull requests need approval
rules.rationale: Workflows triggered from forks run code from the pull request author. Requiring approval for all external contributors prevents unreviewed code from running on your runners.
rules.remediation: Require approval for all external contributors.
rules.manual_check: Screenshot the Actions settings for fork pull request workflows.

rules.title: Self-hosted runners are restricted
rules.rationale: Self-hosted runners are not reset between jobs and often sit inside the corporate network. Any repository that can use a runner can run code on it and reach what it can reach.
rules.remediation: Never allow public repositories to use self-hosted runners. Put runners in groups limited to selected repositories and workflows, and prefer ephemeral runners.
rules.manual_check: Screenshot runner groups in Enterprise and Organization settings > Actions > Runner groups.

references.title: Managing access to self-hosted runners using groups

rules.title: Organization secrets are shared with selected repositories only
rules.rationale: A secret available to all repositories can be read by any workflow in any repository, including new ones and ones with weak protection.
rules.remediation: Change organization secrets to 'Selected repositories', or move them to environment secrets with required reviewers.

rules.title: pull_request_target is not used with untrusted code
rules.rationale: pull_request_target runs with secrets and a write token in the context of the base repository. Checking out or running the pull request's code in such a workflow lets anyone who opens a pull request run code with those privileges.
rules.remediation: Use pull_request instead. If pull_request_target is needed, never check out or execute the pull request head, and keep permissions minimal.

rules.title: Third-party actions are pinned to a commit SHA
rules.rationale: A tag or branch reference runs whatever the action owner publishes under that name next. Pinning to a full commit SHA makes the code that runs immutable.
rules.remediation: Pin third-party actions to a full commit SHA with the version in a comment, and let Dependabot update the pins.

rules.title: Workflows declare token permissions
rules.rationale: Without a permissions block, a workflow gets the default GITHUB_TOKEN permissions, which may include write access. Declaring permissions keeps each workflow at least privilege, whatever the default is.
rules.remediation: Add a top-level 'permissions: contents: read' (or 'permissions: {}') and grant extra permissions per job.

references.title: Use GITHUB_TOKEN for authentication in workflows

rules.title: zizmor finds no workflow vulnerabilities
rules.rationale: zizmor detects template injection, credential persistence, excessive permissions, dangerous triggers and other workflow weaknesses that simple configuration checks cannot see.
rules.remediation: Fix the findings as described in each zizmor audit's documentation, starting with high severity.
rules.manual_check: Run zizmor --offline --format json workflows/ on the collected workflows and pass the result with --zizmor.

rules.title: Secret scanning is enabled
rules.rationale: Secret scanning finds credentials committed to repositories, including history, so they can be revoked before they are abused.
rules.remediation: Enable secret scanning in a security configuration applied to all repositories.

rules.title: Push protection is enabled
rules.rationale: Push protection blocks pushes that contain recognized secrets, so they never reach the repository.
rules.remediation: Enable push protection in the security configuration, and use delegated bypass so bypasses need approval.

rules.title: Dependabot alerts are enabled
rules.rationale: Dependabot alerts report known vulnerabilities in dependencies. Without them, vulnerable libraries go unnoticed.
rules.remediation: Enable the dependency graph and Dependabot alerts in the security configuration for all repositories.

rules.title: Dependabot security updates are enabled
rules.rationale: Security updates open pull requests that fix vulnerable dependencies, which shortens the time from alert to fix.
rules.remediation: Enable Dependabot security updates in the security configuration.

rules.title: Code scanning is enabled
rules.rationale: Code scanning finds vulnerabilities such as injection and unsafe deserialization in the organization's own code before it is merged.
rules.remediation: Enable CodeQL default setup through the security configuration, or add an advanced CodeQL workflow for languages that need it.
rules.manual_check: Repositories may have default setup enabled outside a security configuration. Check Organization > Security > Coverage.

rules.title: New repositories get a security configuration by default
rules.rationale: Without a default configuration, every new repository starts with secret scanning, push protection and Dependabot off until someone remembers to turn them on.
rules.remediation: Set a security configuration as default for new private and internal repositories (for EMU, 'all' or 'private and internal'), and enforce it.

rules.title: No open secret scanning alerts
rules.rationale: An open secret scanning alert is a credential that is, or was, readable by everyone with access to the repository. It must be assumed compromised until it is revoked.
rules.remediation: Revoke and rotate each secret, then close the alert as revoked. Removing it from the code alone is not enough.

rules.title: No open critical or high Dependabot alerts
rules.rationale: Critical and high vulnerabilities in dependencies are often exploitable with public exploits.
rules.remediation: Update or replace the affected dependencies, starting with critical alerts in deployed applications. Set a remediation deadline per severity.

rules.title: No open critical or high code scanning alerts
rules.rationale: Critical and high code scanning alerts are likely vulnerabilities in the organization's own code.
rules.remediation: Triage and fix critical and high alerts. Dismiss false positives with a reason so the backlog stays meaningful.

rules.title: Webhooks use a secret and verified TLS
rules.rationale: Without a secret, the receiver cannot verify that a delivery came from GitHub. Without TLS verification, deliveries, which can contain code and metadata, can be intercepted.
rules.remediation: Set a random secret on every webhook and verify the signature in the receiver. Use HTTPS with certificate verification enabled.

rules.title: Deploy keys are read-only
rules.rationale: A deploy key with write access can push to the repository. It is not tied to a person and does not pass through SSO, so a leaked key is hard to trace.
rules.remediation: Make deploy keys read-only. Use a GitHub App with scoped permissions where write access is needed.

rules.title: GitHub Apps with write access are limited to selected repositories
rules.rationale: An app installed on all repositories with write permissions can change any repository, including new ones. A compromise of the app or its private key affects the whole organization.
rules.remediation: Install apps on selected repositories only, and review whether each write permission is needed.

references.title: Reviewing and modifying installed GitHub Apps

rules.title: Production environments are protected
rules.rationale: Environment secrets and deployment rights are only as protected as the environment. Without reviewers or branch rules, any branch, including one from an unreviewed change, can deploy to production.
rules.remediation: Require reviewers for production environments and limit deployments to protected branches or tags.

rules.title: Audit log is streamed to a SIEM
rules.rationale: The audit log API keeps a limited history and is not monitored. Streaming sends events to the SIEM for retention, alerting and correlation with other logs.
rules.remediation: Configure audit log streaming to the SIEM, include Git events where relevant, and alert on the event types in this report.
rules.manual_check: Screenshot Enterprise settings > Audit log > Log streaming, and compare audit-log-web.ndjson with the SIEM for the same period.

references.title: Streaming the audit log for your enterprise

rules.title: Push protection bypasses are reviewed
rules.rationale: A bypass means a user pushed a detected secret deliberately. Each bypass needs a reason, and the secret usually needs rotation.
rules.remediation: Follow up on each bypass with the user. Enable delegated bypass so bypasses require approval.

references.title: Audit log events for your enterprise

rules.title: Removal or override of branch protection is reviewed
rules.rationale: Deleting rulesets or branch protection, or overriding them, removes the review gate. Attackers and insiders do this before pushing changes.
rules.remediation: Confirm each event with the actor and alert on these events in the SIEM.

references.title: Audit log events for your enterprise

rules.title: Security features are not turned off
rules.rationale: Turning off secret scanning, push protection, Dependabot or code scanning removes detection, sometimes to get a change through.
rules.remediation: Confirm each event, re-enable the feature, and enforce the security configuration so repositories cannot turn it off.

references.title: Audit log events for your enterprise

rules.title: Repository visibility changes, deletions and transfers are reviewed
rules.rationale: Visibility changes widen access to code; deletions and transfers remove it from the organization. These are rare and should be expected.
rules.remediation: Confirm each event with the actor, and restrict these actions to organization owners (POL-02, POL-03).

references.title: Audit log events for your enterprise

rules.title: Self-hosted runner registrations
rules.rationale: New self-hosted runners extend where workflow code runs. Registrations should match known infrastructure.
rules.remediation: Confirm that each runner belongs to managed infrastructure.

references.title: Audit log events for your enterprise

rules.title: Copilot seats are in use
rules.rationale: Unused seats cost money and keep access to Copilot features for people who may no longer need them.
rules.remediation: Remove seats unused for 60 days, or assign Copilot through IdP-synced teams so access follows role changes.

references.title: Reviewing user activity data for Copilot
